I've just been lying on my back staring at the crack in the plaster above my bed, scrolling the same three apps until my thumb aches and my eyes burn. The battery's on nineteen percent. Orange. It'll be dead by morning if I'm not careful. I am never careful.

The text comes in sharp. A single buzz. Three red drops. 🩸🩸🩸.

I sit up so fast the blood leaves my head.

I read it again. Astra. No words. Just the blood. Three of them, lined up like evidence. Like a signature at the bottom of a confession.

My first thought isn't a thought, it's a drop in my stomach, heavy and fast. My second thought is her stepdad. He's not a film villain, he's just a dickhead who drinks Stella and thinks the hallway belongs to him, but still. He's there. He's always there. My third thought is a nosebleed that won't stop. My fourth is worse. I think about her period. She's texted me before about cramps that made her white as a sheet, about bleeding through in Year 10 assembly and running out like a fire alarm. She's got heavy ones. Bad enough that she keeps a whole kit in her bag like she's preparing for surgery. But three drops. Just three drops. No words. No "lol" to soften it. No "sorry" after.

I call. It rings twice and cuts to voicemail. I call again. Nothing. Just her stupid voice, flat and recorded: "You know what to do." I don't. I never have.

I get out of bed and my feet are freezing. The carpet's thin and I can feel the floorboards underneath, ridges and nails. Mum's at work, night shift at the distribution warehouse, won't be back till six with the milk and the quiet. The house is that specific kind of empty where you can hear the fridge hum like it's judging your choices. I pull on my joggers and the hoodie from the back of the chair. It smells like the Co-op, plastic and reduced pastry. I check the pockets. A broken pen lid. A till receipt for a meal deal. No tissues. Nothing useful.

I check my banking app. Two pound thirty-four. The bus is one eighty. That leaves fifty-four p for absolutely fuck all. I can't get an Uber. I can't get a taxi. I can't even run there; it's three miles and my trainers have a hole in the right toe. I get my coat anyway. The zip's been broken since year nine so I hold it shut with one hand tucked in.

Outside it's that fine rain that isn't really rain, more like the air's gone damp and cold. The streetlights are orange and buzzing. One of them's out, flickering like a heartbeat. I walk to the bus stop because I can't afford to stand still and get colder. The N47 comes every forty minutes if you're lucky. I am not lucky but I am patient. I've got the patience of someone who can't afford alternatives.

The bus turns up smelling of chips and defeat. The driver is the one with the beard. He knows me, doesn't say anything. I tap my card and it declines the first time, beeping red. I tap again, slower, praying. Accepted. One pound eighty gone. I climb upstairs. There's a man in the front seat eating chips from a polystyrene tray. Vinegar smell. He doesn't look up. I sit behind him and watch the town go past through smeared glass. Closed Spar. Shut kebab shop with the metal shutters down. A fox that stops under a lamp and stares at us like we're the idiots. The chip man licks his fingers one by one.

I rehearse what I'm going to say. I'm going to be calm. I'm going to say, "You scared the shit out of me," and then I'm going to see what her face does. If she's got a bruise I'll know. If she's holding her arm weird I'll know. If she's pale, if she's shaking, if she's high. I know the shape of her bad nights. I used to be the person she texted when they happened. Not just emoji. Paragraphs. Voice notes at two in the morning. I used to get off the night bus for her and not think about the fare. That was before. Before what, I don't know. We didn't fall out. We just fell off.

Her estate is the newish kind, semi-detached, every third house with a half-inflated birthday banner or a football flag hanging sad in the wet. Her light's on upstairs. Yellow curtain. The stepdad's car is in the drive, big silver thing. I stand in the front garden and look up. I don't want to ring the doorbell because then he wakes up and then it's a whole thing, him in the doorway, Astra mortified, me standing there like a charity case. I pick up gravel from the flowerbed and throw it. It pings off the glass too loud. I wince. I throw another one softer, a flat chip of slate. I hiss her name. "Astra." It comes out pathetic, like a leak. "Astra."

The window slides up. She leans out. She's got her hoodie on, hood down, hair in a greasy knot. She's not bleeding. She's not crying. She's annoyed.

"What the fuck," she says.

I open my mouth and nothing comes out. I'm looking for blood. Her lip. Her hands. Her eyes. There's nothing.

"Robin," she says. "It's half past midnight."

"I got your text," I say. My voice sounds wrong. Too loud. "The blood. Three of them."

She blinks. "What?"

"The emoji. 🩸🩸🩸. You sent it to me."

She looks at me for a long second. Then she laughs. It's not a nice laugh. It's a tired one, the kind that means you're an idiot and she's too exhausted to explain why.

"Oh my God," she says. "You're dead. That's what it means. You're dead. In the game."

I just stand there. The rain's getting into my collar, running down my neck.

"What game," I say, except it's not a question. I already know. I know about Felix and his stupid fucking WhatsApp groups. I've seen the statuses. I've ignored them.

"Bleedout," she says. She yawns. Actually yawns, showing her back teeth. "Felix started it. Water pistols. Five quid in. I got you. You're my target. So. 🩸🩸🩸. You're dead."

I look at her. I look at the gravel in my hand. I drop it into the wet grass.

"You sent me three blood drops," I say. "At midnight."

"Yeah, it's my signature." She's leaning on the windowsill now, bored, chin on her hand. "I sent it to five people. You're the only one who came."

There's a beat. The fox from the high street couldn't be more right about me.

"You're a fucking idiot," she says, but not mean. Just stating a fact. Like the weather. "Go home, Rob."

She slides the window down. The light goes off. The curtain doesn't move.

I stand in the wet garden for another minute. My socks are soaked through from the grass. I didn't even notice. I walk back to the bus stop and wait twenty-three minutes for the N47 going the other way. The chip man is gone. There's just me and a girl who keeps coughing into her sleeve and a man who smells like lager.

On the bus home I think about Astra's voice. It was thick. Like she'd been talking before I got there, or crying after, or like she'd just swallowed something hot. But the light went off so fast, and she yawned, and she looked fine. She looked fine. I push the thought down into my stomach where it can keep the other things company. I focus on the £1.80. That's a real number. That's something I can be angry about instead of the other thing. The rain on the window makes streaks like fingers. I don't look at them. I count the stops till mine.
step_outputs.7:
I wake up to the sound of Mum shutting the front door. Six AM. She’s left a fiver on the kitchen counter with a Post-it that says “bus” in her blocky capitals. I stare at it for a while. The counter’s sticky where she spilled squash last night and wiped it with a dishcloth that needed burning six months ago. I put the fiver in my pocket and eat a bowl of cereal dry because the milk’s gone off. It smells like wallpaper paste. I eat it anyway.

My blazer’s still damp from the rain. I put it on and the lining clings to my sleeve like a wet tongue. There’s the stain on the left lapel, the biro mark from year nine, but now there’s also a dark patch near the hem where I leaned against the bus window. It smells like damp dog and Co-op disinfectant. I have two hours of sleep singing behind my eyes, a high-pitched whine that makes everything too bright.

The walk to the bus stop is the same as always. Pavement slabs cracked like dried mud. A crisp packet skittering across the road. The 47 comes on time for once, driven by a woman who doesn’t look at my pass. I sit at the back and rest my forehead against the glass. It vibrates. I think about Astra’s window sliding shut. I think about the fiver Mum left and how it’s already gone on bus fare. I think about nothing.

School hits like a fluorescent slap. The humanities block smells of floor wax and anxiety. I’m late to registration because I stopped at the toilet to piss and ended up staring at the graffiti on the cubicle door for five minutes. Someone’s written “Felix is a melt” in black marker and underneath, in different handwriting, “agreed.” I don’t know who wrote either bit but I agree with both.

Our registration room is a Portakabin that’s been here since before I started. It’s got that temporary-building permanence, the scuffed lino and the heater that sounds like a dying animal. I slump into my seat. The chair’s wonky and the desk has someone’s old gum stuck to the underside. I pick at it with my thumbnail. Around me people are talking about the weekend, about someone’s cousin’s party, about TikToks I haven’t seen because my data’s capped and I can’t afford to refresh.

Felix is standing at the front. He’s not meant to stand at the front—Mr. Vance is meant to be here—but Mr. Vance is limping, I heard, something about a knee, so Felix is holding court like the little king he thinks he is. He’s got his Head Boy badge on, polished, and he’s holding his phone like it’s the Magna Carta.

“Gents,” he says. He says gents. “And ladies. Settle.”

Nobody settles. But they quieten because they want to see what he’s doing. He turns his phone around. It’s a WhatsApp group chat called “Bleedout Official.” The wallpaper is a picture of him doing a thumbs-up next to the school sign.

“Over half-term,” Felix says, “I set up a little tournament. Assassination. Water pistols. Five quid entry. Winner takes all.”

He beams. He looks like a baby who’s just learned to clap. Someone at the back says “sick” without meaning it.

“It’s fully booked,” Felix says. “Fourteen entrants. Bracket’s live. I’ve just added a few latecomers.”

My phone buzzes in my pocket. I pull it out, already knowing. There it is: Felix Addison has added you to Bleedout Official. The group icon is the same thumbs-up photo. I scroll up. There’s the rules, typed by Felix in paragraphs with no punctuation, full of words like “immunity” and “safe zones” and “headshots only count if witnessed.” It’s pathetic. It’s also got fourteen members and a pinned message saying “£5 bank transfer to Felix A. Sort code 20-45-…”

I look up. Felix is looking at me. Not with malice. He doesn’t know who I am. He just sees a new number, a new fiver.

Then I see my target.

It’s in a Google Doc link, pinned below the rules. I click it. The page loads slow, pixel by pixel, because the signal in the Portakabin is held together by prayer. Then there it is: a spreadsheet. Names in two columns. Hunter. Target.

My name is next to Astra’s.

I stare at it. The screen’s cracked in the top corner so her name has a little hairline fracture running through it. Astra Moore. My target.

The bell goes. Everyone stands up, scraping chairs. Felix is still talking about safe zones—canteen’s out, toilets are in, staff block is automatic disqualification—but I’m not listening. I’m looking at the door.

Astra walks in. She’s late too. She’s got her hoodie under her blazer, which is against uniform code, and her eyeliner is smudged at the left corner. She doesn’t look at Felix. She looks at me. For a second, nothing. Then she smiles. Not a nice smile. A corner of her mouth goes up, and she lifts her chin, and she walks past my desk so close I can smell the vanilla body spray she’s used since Year 8.

She doesn’t say anything. Doesn’t mime a gun or wink or do anything cinematic. Just that smile, and gone.

My face goes hot. The damp lining of my blazer is freezing against my wrist. I sit back down even though the bell’s gone, even though people are pushing past me. I look at the spreadsheet again. Astra Moore. I think about last night. The gravel in my hand. Her yawning mouth. You’re the only one who came.

I don’t have a water pistol. I don’t have five quid to waste on Felix’s stupid game. I don’t know the rules and I don’t care. But I’m going to play. I’m going to play because she smiled like that, like I’m a joke, like I’m nothing, like I didn’t get on the night bus for her.

I stand up. My knee clicks. I walk out into the corridor and the light’s too bright and everything smells of floor wax.

Break happens in the canteen because it’s raining again and they’ve declared the field a mud pit. I buy a coffee from the machine, the kind that tastes like burnt rubber and costs £1.10, which leaves me with three pound coins and some change from Mum’s fiver. I’m holding it too tight, walking through the crush of bodies near the toaster, when someone shoulder-checks me. I don’t see who. The lid pops off and coffee goes down my front, a hot stripe across my shirt and tie.

“Shit,” I say, out loud, too loud.

I’m standing there with brown liquid dripping onto my shoes and a blister forming on my collarbone. People are laughing, not at me specifically, just the general laughter of people who are dry and warm and not holding a ruined coffee. I’m about to walk to the toilets to stick my head under the tap when a hand appears.

It’s holding a napkin. A thin, papery one from the canteen dispenser.

I look up. It’s Cam. Cam from Chemistry, back row, always drawing hexagons in the margin. They’re not looking at my face. They’re looking at the coffee stain, and their expression is the same one they use when a Bunsen burner won’t light. Mild inconvenience. Nothing more.

I take the napkin. “Cheers.”

Cam nods. They’re holding a coffee too, untouched, in their other hand. They don’t say “alliance.” They don’t say “I heard you got Astra” or “Felix is a prick.” They just stand there, sip their coffee, and look out at the rain hitting the windows.

I wipe uselessly at my shirt. The napkin disintegrates into wet lumps.

“Your ear’s wet,” Cam says.

I touch my right ear. Coffee. Of course.

“Other one,” Cam says.

I touch my left. Also wet. I don’t know when that happened.

We stand there. The rain comes down. Somewhere across the hall, Felix is laughing, a honking sound that carries even over the toaster alarm. I look at Cam. Cam looks at the floor. We don’t agree to anything. We don’t need to. We’re just two people who got coffee on themselves and didn’t run away.

I crumple the napkin in my fist. Astra’s still out there, probably in the humanities corridor, probably smirking at someone else now. I think about the £5 I don’t have. I think about the water pistol I need to buy.

My phone buzzes. A message in Bleedout Official. Felix: Remember gents, first bleed by Friday.

I don’t reply. But I don’t leave the group either.
step_outputs.8:
I go to the corner shop at lunch because it’s the only place within walking distance that sells anything resembling a weapon. It’s one of those shops that smells of dusty bread and dishwasher tablets, run by a man who’s been watching the same small TV since 2008. I stand in the aisle with the toys and the light bulbs and the off-brand batteries. There are three water pistols on a clip-strip. One’s neon green, one’s pink with a mermaid on it, and one’s shaped like a dolphin. I take the green one. It’s £2.49, which leaves me with just over two quid for the rest of the week. The man puts it in a thin plastic bag that immediately gets a hole in it.

By the time I’m back at the school gates, my blazer pocket is wet. Not damp. Wet. The pistol is leaking from somewhere near the trigger, a slow, cold seep that’s spreading across the lining and onto my thigh. I try to hold it away from my body, walking with my arm slightly out like I’ve injured it. People look at me. I look at the floor. The floor is speckled linoleum and old gum and the shadows of people who know exactly how much I’ve just spent on a piece of neon plastic that doesn’t even hold water.

The humanities block is where Astra usually eats. She doesn’t go to the canteen anymore because she says the chips smell like feet. She sits on the low wall by the fire exit, near the bins, with her hood up and her knees drawn in. I see her from the corner. She’s alone, scrolling her phone, a half-eaten sandwich next to her. The wall is damp from the morning rain. Her blazer’s got mud on the hem.

I approach from the side. My plan is non-existent. My plan is to walk up, point the pistol, and pull the trigger. That’s the whole plan. My heart is doing something arrhythmic in my chest. The leak in my pocket has reached my hip bone. I take the pistol out. It’s slippery. Water runs down my wrist and into my sleeve.

Astra looks up.

I aim. I pull the trigger. It makes a squeaking sound and a thin, apologetic dribble comes out, misses her by roughly two feet, and patters onto the pavement between us. Then the whole front seal gives way and the rest of the water dumps directly down my own forearm, soaking my cuff, my watch strap, and the front of my shirt.

Astra stares at me. She doesn’t move. She doesn’t flinch. She just looks at the green pistol in my hand, then at the dark patch spreading across my chest, then back at my face.

“What,” she says. Not a question. A diagnosis.

I stand there with water dripping off my elbow. The pistol is empty now. Completely empty. I spent two pound forty-nine on two seconds of pathetic noise and personal dampness.

“You’re soaking,” Astra says.

“I’m aware.”

She picks up her sandwich. “Buy a better one,” she says, and bites into it. White bread. Cheap ham. She chews, looking at me with no expression at all, then stands up, brushes the wall-damp off her trousers, and walks away toward the toilets. She doesn’t look back. I watch her go. The water in my sleeve is cold. It’s seeping into my armpit.

I become aware that I am not alone.

Cam is standing by the bins. They are also wet. Not as wet as me, but there’s a dark patch down their front, and their hair is stuck to their forehead in a way that suggests someone has recently emptied a vessel over their head. They’re holding a Super Soaker. It’s enormous, military-grade, the kind of thing that requires two hands and a shoulder strap. It’s also got a sticker on it that says “Ages 6+.”

Cam looks at my pistol. Then at their own. Then back at me.

“Yours leaks,” they say.

“Yours works too well.”

“They’ve got a hose in the PE block,” Cam says. “I asked. Mr. Dhingra said no. Then I did it anyway when his back was turned.”

They hold up the Super Soaker. Water drips from the nozzle onto their shoe.

I look down at my green plastic catastrophe. “I’m going to wring this out,” I say.

“Toilets,” Cam says.

We walk together. Not like allies. Like two people who have been rained on by their own choices.

The toilets by the maths corridor are the worst in the school. The door handle is sticky. The floor is wet already, though not from water pistols. The smell is industrial urinal cake and something else, something organic and despairing. We go to the sinks. I take my blazer off. The inside pocket is a dark, misshapen bloom. I try to wring it out and a thin stream of water runs into the basin. Cam stands next to me, wringing their sleeve. They’re very methodical about it, twisting from the wrist down, then the elbow, then the shoulder. Like a recipe.

I look at us in the mirror. Two damp teenagers in a council-school toilet. I look like I’ve pissed myself. Cam looks like they fell in a canal. If this is a heist film, we’re the henchmen who get caught in the first act.

“Felix,” I say. “He’s running this like he’s Bond.”

Cam doesn’t look up. “He’s running it like a wanker.”

I laugh, a short, surprised bark. It echoes off the tiles.

We go into the cubicles because someone’s coming in. I take the middle one, Cam takes the end. I sit on the closed lid with my wet blazer in my lap. My trousers are sticking to the back of my thighs. I can hear Cam breathing, a steady in-and-out. Outside, the hand dryer starts, the old-fashioned kind that just wheezes warm air and bacteria.

Then the door bangs open again.

“—not even that much,” Felix is saying. His voice carries. Everything about Felix carries. “Like, twenty quid. Maybe twenty-five. I’ll put it back when I win, obviously.”

Another voice. One of the Year 12s, I think. A boy with a laugh like a drain. “You spent the entry fees?”

“Borrowed,” Felix says. I hear him walk past my cubicle. His shoes are those clean white trainers that stay clean for about three days. “I borrowed it. Cash flow. It’s networking, mate. Nando’s with the rugby lot. You’ve got to invest to accumulate.”

“Rugby lot don’t even go here,” the Year 12 says.

“They will,” Felix says. He stops near the sinks. I can see a sliver of his reflection in the gap under the cubicle door. His white shoes. “Anyway, I’m exempt from being hunted till the semis. Wrote the rules. Fair’s fair.”

The hand dryer stops. There’s a pause.

“You’re exempt,” the Year 12 repeats. Flat.

“Natural advantage,” Felix says. His voice has that honking laugh buried in it, the one that escapes when he thinks he’s said something clever. “Plus I’m the only one with the spreadsheet. If anyone asks, I’ll say it was a software glitch.”

“Mate,” the Year 12 says. “That’s theft.”

“It’s entrepreneurship,” Felix says. The tap runs. I hear him washing his hands for exactly the recommended twenty seconds, because Felix follows rules when they suit him. “Gents, I’m telling you. Builds character.”

The door bangs. They’re gone.

I sit in the cubicle with my wet blazer. The plastic pistol is on the floor between my feet, a neon green oblong of failure. I look at it. I look at the gap under the door where Felix’s white shoes were.

My hands are shaking. Not from fear. From something smaller and hotter. Twenty quid. Maybe twenty-five. That’s five people’s entry fees. That’s Mum’s night shift. That’s my Saturday at the till, scanning meal deals for people who don’t look at me. And he spent it on chicken. Not a ledger. Not a conspiracy. Just Nando’s with people who don’t even go to our school.

I kick the cubicle door. It rattles in its frame. The sound is satisfyingly cheap.

From the end cubicle, Cam’s voice comes, steady and unsurprised.

“Toilets,” they say. “Not a murder scene.”

I lean back against the cistern. My shirt is cold and my hands are shaking and I want to burn Felix’s clean white shoes. But I can’t. Because this isn’t a film. This is just a shit school with a shit game and a shit boy who thinks £25 makes him a CEO.

I pick up the pistol. Water sloshes in the hollow barrel.

“We’re getting it back,” I say.

There’s a pause. Cam flushes, even though they haven’t used the toilet. It’s the only reply I get.
step_outputs.9:
Wednesday smells like chips and rain. The canteen is that particular shade of beige that makes everyone look ill, lit by tubes that buzz overhead. I’m in the queue with a tray, holding a warm carton of juice and a cheese roll that’s been compressed by its own packaging into a dense, yellowish log. I haven’t bought the juice. I found it in my bag from last week. It’s slightly swollen. I’m going to drink it anyway.

I see the ketchup before I see the person holding it. A red arc, sudden and bright, across the lino near the hot food counter. Then a scream that’s not a scream, more of a yelp, and someone laughing, and then Mr. Vance is there.

He’s limping already from whatever happened Monday—someone said he slipped in the corridor, someone else said football injury, but he’s been moving like a damaged rocking horse since registration. He’s holding a tray with a shepherd’s pie and a mug of tea. He sees the ketchup on the floor. He tries to navigate around it. His bad knee goes. He reaches for the nearest stable object, which is Mrs. Gorman, the dinner lady, and they both go down in a slow, awful collapse of limbs and polyester.

The mug breaks. The tea goes everywhere, a lake of beige across the ketchup. Mrs. Gorman is on her back, blinking, holding a ladle like a weapon. Mr. Vance is on one knee, his face a strange purplish colour, holding his other knee with both hands.

“Right,” he says, into the sudden quiet. “Well. This is what we’re doing now, is it.”

Nobody laughs. It’s too pathetic to laugh at. Someone helps Mrs. Gorman up. She’s fine, just shocked, patting her hairnet. Mr. Vance stays on the floor for a long moment, looking at the ketchup like it’s personally offended him. Then he gets up, slowly, and the limp is worse. He doesn’t shout. He just looks at all of us, several hundred teenagers holding our breaths over our trays, and says, “Assembly. Year 12 and 13. Five minutes.”

He walks out, dragging his leg slightly. Mrs. Gorman picks up the mug handle. It’s the only bit left.

The assembly is in the main hall, which smells of floor polish and other people’s coats. We sit on the folding chairs that pinch your fingers if you’re not careful. Mr. Vance is on stage with the Head, who looks like she’s been interrupted from something important, possibly a nap. Mr. Vance doesn’t speak. The Head does.

“Some of you,” she says, “appear to be engaged in an organised activity involving water pistols and”—she looks at a piece of paper—“condiments. This stops now. The canteen is not a warzone. Mr. Vance has been injured. There will be no more of this… Bleedout.”

She says it like it’s a word she’s translating from another language.

“Any student found carrying a water pistol, a water bottle used as a water pistol, or any condiment-based weapon, will receive an automatic detention. This includes mayonnaise.”

Nobody knew mayonnaise was involved. Someone at the back giggles. The Head glares until it dies.

We file out. The game is banned, which means it immediately becomes more interesting. By the time I’m back in the corridor, three people have already been assassinated in the toilets. I see a Year 12 sprinting out of the boys’ with his hood up and a massive grin, water dripping from his chin. It’s raining outside, so everyone’s already damp anyway. The ban just means the dampness now feels illicit.

I don’t know why I look for Astra. I just know she wasn’t in assembly. Her form group was there—saw them near the back, one of them eating crisps—but Astra’s seat was empty. I walk the corridors with my cheese roll in my pocket, getting warm and flattened against my thigh. I check the usual spots. The wall by the fire exit is empty, just a puddle where someone sat. The LRC is full of Year 11s pretending to revise. The sixth-form common room has a sign on the door saying CLOSED DUE TO INCIDENT.

I find her in the disabled toilet near the drama block. It’s the one with the broken lock that everyone uses when they need to cry or vape or both. The door’s shut but not latched properly. I can see her shoe through the gap. Black trainer, white sock, tapping.

I knock. No answer. I push the door.

Astra is sitting on the closed lid, not the floor, which is something. She’s got her blazer off, her white shirt in her hands, dabbing at a red stain on the front with a handful of toilet paper. The paper is dissolving into pink mush. There’s ketchup in her hair, too, a single red streak above her ear where someone must have flicked it, or she walked into the arc. She looks up. Her face is not crying. It’s just tired. The kind of tired that sits behind your eyes and makes everything too bright.

“What,” she says.

I don’t have a wet wipe. I don’t carry them. But I remember the tiny packet that came with the meal deal last week, tucked into the front pocket of my bag. I dig it out. It’s branded with the Co-op logo. I hold it out.

She looks at it. Then at me.

“You came,” she says. Not like it’s nice. Like it’s an accusation.

“You’ve got ketchup,” I say.

She takes the wipe. Pulls it out. It’s small, insufficient for the stain, but she dabs at it anyway, mechanically, not looking at what she’s doing.

“I sent it to five people,” she says. The wipe is turning orange. “The text. That night. Five people.”

I lean against the sink. The porcelain is cold through my shirt.

“You’re the only one who came,” she says.

“The night bus,” I say. “One eighty. I counted.”

She looks at me then. Properly. Her eyes are red-rimmed but dry. She’s re-applied her eyeliner in the mirror above the sink; I can see the black smear on the cardboard edge where she wiped the pencil. She did it carefully, evenly, the way you do when you’ve been crying and need to armour up before anyone sees.

“You’re a fucking idiot,” she says. Softly. No heat. “I didn’t need you to come. I didn’t ask you to come. You just… you always have to make everything a thing, Rob. You always have to be the one who—” She stops. The wipe rips. She holds two pieces of damp paper. “You wasted your money. You wasted your night. For what? For a game?”

“It wasn’t a game at midnight,” I say. My voice comes out higher than I want. “It was three blood drops. No words. What was I meant to think?”

“That I was being dramatic? That I was drunk? That I was playing a stupid game with my stupid mates and you’re not my mate anymore so why did you—” She stops again. She balls up the paper. Throws it at the bin. It misses, hits the floor, sticks there.

“You’re not my mate anymore,” she says, to the wall.

I feel the cheese roll in my pocket, warm and dense. I feel the damp patch on my hip where the pistol leaked yesterday. I feel the £1.80 like a coin pressed into my sternum.

“I got on the bus,” I say. “I didn’t have to. I could’ve stayed in bed. I could’ve texted back ‘lol.’ I got on the bus because you sent me blood, Astra. Actual blood. What the fuck else was I meant to do?”

She picks at her thumbnail. The skin around it is raw, bitten. She’s got a scab forming on the side of her index finger. She pulls at it until it bleeds, a small, bright bead.

“You could’ve known I was fine,” she says.

“How?”

“Because I’m always fine,” she says. “That’s the point.”

We look at each other. The fluorescent light above the mirror flickers, a tiny stutter. The tap drips. Outside, someone runs past the door, laughing, their shoes squeaking on the lino.

“I’m fine too,” I say. It sounds like a lie, which it is.

She puts her blazer back on. The ketchup stain is still there, a dark smear between the buttons. She doesn’t button it. She just stands up, checks her phone, and walks past me. She doesn’t touch me. She doesn’t say thanks for the wipe. She stops at the door.

“The bus,” she says, not turning around. “One eighty. You should’ve saved it.”

Then she’s gone. The door swings shut, doesn’t click, swings open again a few inches. I stand in the disabled toilet with the smell of chemical air freshener and pink toilet paper. I look at the bin. I look at the mirror. I look at my own face, which is grey and slightly too thin and has a spot forming on my chin.

I turn on the tap. The water is cold, almost painfully so. I wash my hands. I wash them properly, the way they taught us in primary school, between the fingers, under the nails, the full twenty seconds. The soap smells like cheap lemons. My hands go red, then white. I keep washing them. I wash them until they’re raw and the water running off them is clean and I can’t feel my fingertips anymore.
step_outputs.10:
I find Cam at the bike sheds. They’re not smoking, though the bike sheds are for smoking. They’re just standing there with their hood up, looking at a pigeon that’s trapped itself between two rusted BMXs. The pigeon is panicking in that dull, repetitive way that pigeons do. Cam is watching it with no particular urgency.

"We're going through his bag," I say.

Cam doesn't look at me. "Whose?"

"Felix's."

"Why?"

I don't have a good answer. I have a receipt-shaped hole in my afternoon and a general sense that someone should suffer. "He spent the money."

"What money?"

"The fivers. For the game."

Cam nods, still watching the pigeon. "On chicken."

"On chicken."

The pigeon escapes, a clatter of grey wings. Cam turns to me. Their face is the same as always. Sleepy. Unbothered. "Okay," they say.

We don't formulate a plan. We just walk.

The astroturf is behind the sports block, that bright green plastic grass that smells like warmed-up chemicals and teenage sweat. Felix is playing five-a-side with the rugby lot, or what Felix thinks is the rugby lot. They're mostly just boys in socks who like shouting. Felix is in goal, which means he's standing near the fence with his hands on his knees, looking important. His bag is next to the post. It's a black Nike rucksack, clean, with a tiny Head Boy badge clipped to the strap like a medal.

We approach from the blind side. The game is loud, full of meaty thuds and barked instructions. No one looks at us. We're not invisible; we're just not interesting.

Cam crouches first. They unzip the bag like they're opening a lunchbox. No drama. No furtive glances. Just two teenagers looking through another teenager's possessions on a Thursday afternoon because there's nothing better to do.

I kneel. The astroturf is damp and the moisture seeps through my trouser knees immediately. I can smell Felix before I find him: Lynx Africa, the sports block changing rooms, that particular clean smell of someone who has never had to worry about smelling bad.

The bag is disappointingly normal. A geography textbook with corners like chewed bread. A pencil case with his name written inside in Tippex. A water bottle with the school's logo, full and unopened. A tub of gum. A spare tie, rolled tight.

Then: a brown envelope, A4, folded in half. Written on the front in thick black marker: BLEEDOUT £££. The letters are careful, almost primary-school neat. Felix has drawn a tiny pound sign with two lines.

I pull it out. It's light. Too light. It should have the weight of fourteen five-pound notes, or at least a decent handful of change. It feels like paper. Just paper.

I open it.

Inside is a receipt from Nando's. Crumpled. The paper is thin and the ink is faded in a stripe where it's been folded. I smooth it out on my knee.

Half chicken, extra hot. Creamy mash. Spicy rice. Two soft drinks. £23.40.

There's a stamp. CARD PAYMENT APPROVED. There's a time: 19:43, last Friday. The day after he launched the game. He didn't even wait.

I stare at it. £23.40. That's four people's entry fees. Almost five. That's Mum finishing her shift with her feet swelling in her trainers. That's my Saturday, standing at the till, saying "would you like a bag?" to people who don't look up.

Cam leans over. They read it. Their expression doesn't change. "He got a drink," they say. "Two drinks."

"He took someone."

"Rugby lot."

"Rugby lot don't even go here."

"I know," Cam says.

I should feel triumphant. I should feel like a detective. Instead I feel small and grubby, crouched on fake grass with someone else's receipt in my hand. The triumph is already curdling into something else. Embarrassment. The kind that comes from caring about something no one else cares about.

"Photo," Cam says.

They hand me their phone. It's cracked across the camera lens in a spiderweb pattern. I line up the shot. My thumb goes over the corner. I take the picture. It's blurry. I take another. In this one, the receipt is readable but there's a massive thumb-shaped shadow on the left side and a sliver of my trouser leg at the bottom. It looks like evidence from a crime scene investigated by an incompetent child.

"Send it to me," I say.

Cam does. The message takes thirty seconds to arrive because the signal by the astroturf is weak. I open the Bleedout group chat. Felix's thumbs-up icon. Fourteen members. I attach the photo. I type: "The prize fund."

I stare at the screen. The cursor blinks. I press send.

The message goes. One grey tick. Then two. Then blue. Delivered. Read by Felix. Read by someone else. Read by another.

I wait.

The five-a-side game continues. Felix shouts something about marking. A ball hits the fence near my head and I flinch. Cam stands up, brushes their knees. We walk away, back toward the main block, leaving the bag as we found it. I check my phone every four steps. Nothing.

We sit on the wall by the humanities corridor. It's cold. My hands are shaking slightly from the damp astroturf. I check the chat. No replies. Just my message sitting there, the blurry photo of the Nando's receipt, my thumb in the corner like a signature.

Fifteen minutes. The period bell goes. People spill out of doors. I check again. Nothing.

I go to my next lesson. History. We learn about something—I don't know what. I spend the hour with my phone in my lap, brightness down, refreshing. The message has been read by eleven people. Twelve. Thirteen. No replies.

In the last ten minutes of the lesson, my phone buzzes. I jolt so hard the person next to me looks over.

It's a meme. A crying cat, the one with tears streaming down its face, photoshopped onto a picture of a Nando's plate. Sent by someone called Kyle in Year 12. Not even in our year. He's just in the group because Felix added everyone he had in his contacts.

Below it, someone else: "RIP 💀"

Then: "Extra hot tho"

Then: "Felix u melt"

Then nothing. No outrage. No demands for the money back. Just four messages and then the chat goes quiet again. I stare at it. I scroll up. My receipt photo is there, my thumb in the corner, looking pathetic. The read receipts glow blue and indifferent.

I sit in History with my phone in my lap and I feel it. The specific, shrinking feeling of being the only person in the room who thought this was important. Felix stole twenty-three pounds and forty pence. He spent it on chicken. And everyone knows, and nobody cares, because it's only twenty-three pounds, and it's only Felix, and it's only a game that was already banned, and the whole thing is too small to matter.

But it matters to me. It matters to me in a way that makes me feel like an idiot. Like Robin on the night bus. Like the only person who shows up.

The lesson ends. I put my phone in my pocket. It stays silent. The Bleedout chat stays silent. Outside, it's started raining again, the fine, soaking kind. I walk to the canteen and buy nothing. I just stand in the queue for a minute, then leave.

Cam is by the vending machine. They look at me. They don't ask. They already know.

"He's not even replying," I say.

"No," Cam says.

"He's just..."

"Eating," Cam says. "Probably."

I laugh. It comes out wrong, like a cough. Cam offers me a Polo. I take it. It's linty from their pocket. I put it in my mouth and it tastes of chalk and peppermint and the inside of a school bag.

We stand there. The vending machine hums. The fluorescent light above it flickers. Outside, Felix is probably still playing five-a-side, still shouting, still clean and confident and utterly untouched by the fact that everyone knows he's a thief and nobody cares enough to stop him.

My phone stays quiet. The crying cat stares up from the screen, tears frozen mid-stream, laughing at something I don't understand.
step_outputs.11:
Friday is wet break from the start. The sky is that low, colourless grey that makes the corridors feel like they’re underground. At twelve-fifteen someone makes the announcement over the tannoy, the voice crackling and bored: students are to remain indoors due to adverse weather conditions. Everyone cheers because indoors means chaos. The canteen is a furnace of damp uniforms and shouting. The LRC is full of people who don’t want to be found. The corridors smell of steamed polyester.

I go outside anyway. The rain is barely rain, more like a suspended mist that gets inside your collar and stays there. I’ve got the new pistol in my inside pocket. It’s smaller than the green one, clear plastic with an orange nozzle, and it cost £1.99 from the same corner shop. I didn’t take the sticker off. It says “SUMMER FUN” in a curling font. I didn’t take it off because I didn’t look at it properly until I was outside, and then I couldn’t be bothered to go back.

The bike sheds are behind the sports block, a corrugated roof on rusted poles with a couple of bent rails underneath. They smell of rust and old smoke and the sweet, rotten smell of mud that’s been rained on too many times. There are fag ends everywhere, trodden into the ground in a pattern that looks like disease. I walk up slowly. My trainers are already darkening at the toes.

Astra is there. She’s alone, standing under the drip where the roof leaks worst, her hood up, her back to me. She’s on the phone. I can hear her voice before I can hear her words.

“I said I’d pick it up, didn’t I? I said.” A pause. She kicks the ground. Mud splatters her sock, white turning brown. “I’m at school. What do you want me to do, teleport?”

I stop. I’m about ten feet away, half behind the pole. The water pistol is in my hand, hidden against my thigh. My heart is going stupidly fast. I can feel it in my neck.

“Well tell him to go himself,” Astra says. Her voice is sharp but small, the voice of someone who’s used to arguing in whispers. “It’s his prescription. I don’t know why it’s my—” She stops. Listens. “Yeah. Yeah, fine. Fine.”

She hangs up. She stands there for a second with the phone in her hand, looking at the screen. Then she puts it in her pocket and turns around.

She sees me. She doesn’t look surprised. She looks like someone who’s just remembered they left the iron on.

“Rob,” she says.

I step out from behind the pole. The rain is on my face now, fine and cold. I’ve been rehearsing this for two days. In my head, I stride up, I say something cutting, I aim, I fire, she’s dead, I walk away. In my head, it’s clean. It’s a scene.

Instead, I’m standing in mud. The bike shed is leaking on my shoulder. Astra has her coursework folder in her hand, a blue cardboard one with a plastic wallet inside. I can see the edge of paper. Her hood is slipping and her hair is getting wet at the front. She looks tired. She looks like someone who’s been on the phone about a prescription during her lunch break.

The moment stretches. I realise with a horrible clarity how stupid this is. I’m holding a £1.99 water pistol with a SUMMER FUN sticker on it. She’s holding a folder full of work. The rain is coming down. There is no music. There is no slow motion. There is just me, and her, and the wet ground, and the fact that I came all the way out here to shoot her with water.

I raise the pistol anyway.

I pull the trigger.

It’s a better stream than the green one. A thin, aggressive jet that travels maybe four feet and hits her square in the chest. Except she’s holding the folder in front of her chest, hugging it against herself because it’s raining and she’s trying to keep it dry. The water hits the cardboard. It doesn’t hit her. Not really. A splash catches her chin, but the main force of it slaps into the blue folder.

The paper inside blooms.

I see it happen. The ink on the first page—printed text, probably an essay—starts to bleed immediately, the words melting into grey smudges. The cardboard darkens in a star pattern around the point of impact. The plastic wallet does nothing. Water runs down the front and drips onto her shoes.

Astra looks down at her folder. She looks at it for a long time. Then she looks up at me.

She doesn’t shout. She doesn’t swear. She doesn’t even move to wipe the water off her chin. She just stands there, holding her ruined work, and the rain keeps coming, and the leak from the roof keeps dripping behind her, and I feel the pistol going slack in my hand.

“You proper ruined my night, you know,” she says. Her voice is flat. Not angry. Just factual. “Coming over.”

I lower the pistol. The orange nozzle is dripping onto my shoe.

“You sent three blood drops,” I say. My voice sounds small. I hate it. “At midnight.”

“I know what I sent.”

“What was I meant to do? Ignore it?”

“Yes,” she says. “Ignore it. Like everyone else did.”

She adjusts her grip on the folder. The wet cardboard is starting to sag. A drop of dyed ink runs down the edge and onto her thumb.

“I didn’t think you’d actually come,” she says. “That’s the point. I didn’t think anyone would come. And then you did, and you were standing in the garden, and you looked at me like—” She stops. She shakes her head. “Like I owed you something. And I don’t. I don’t owe you that.”

“You sent blood,” I say. “Three times. What was I meant to think?”

“I don’t know,” she says. “That I’m a drama queen? That I’m a mess? That I was pissed and it seemed funny?” She shrugs, one shoulder, the folder cradled against her chest like an injured pet. “You don’t know me anymore, Rob. You don’t get to show up at midnight because you think I’m dying. I’m not your thing to save.”

I stand there with the pistol in my hand. The SUMMER FUN sticker is peeling at the corner. I feel the rain in my hair, running down my neck, pooling in the gap between my collar and my spine. I want to say something huge and cutting. I want to tell her she’s selfish, that she’s cruel, that she uses people like batteries. But the words don’t come. They never do. They sit in my throat like stones.

Astra looks at the folder again. The ink has stopped blooming and started running, thin grey rivers down the blue cardboard. She tucks it under her arm, the wet side against her blazer. She’ll have to do it again. Print it again. Stay up late while her stepdad watches the telly too loud.

“I’ve got to go,” she says. “I need to ask for an extension.”

She walks past me. Not brushing against me, but close enough that I can smell the vanilla body spray mixed with the rain. She doesn’t look back. She walks out from under the bike shed, into the grey, and her hood slips further down, and she doesn’t fix it. She just walks, holding the ruined folder against her chest, her shoes making a wet, rhythmless sound on the path.

I stand there. The pistol drips onto the mud. I look at the ground where she was standing. There’s a fag end, trodden flat, and a wrapper from a Cheestring, and a dark patch where the water from the roof has made a small crater. I step into the crater. My trainer sinks half an inch. The water soaks through the hole in my toe.

I raise the pistol and point it at the rusted pole. I pull the trigger. A thin stream comes out, then a dribble, then nothing. The tank is empty. I keep pulling it anyway. Click. Click. Click. The orange nozzle makes a small, pathetic sound, like a toy running out of batteries.

I stand in the bike sheds and listen to the rain on the corrugated roof. It’s not dramatic. It’s just loud. I think about Astra’s face when she said *I don’t owe you that*. She looked sad. Not guilty. Sad. Like I was the one who’d done something wrong, showing up, caring, being there. Like my caring was a burden she hadn’t asked for and didn’t want.

The bell goes. It’s faint out here, muffled by the rain and the sports block. I don’t move. I stand there until my hands are red and my sock is soaked through the hole and the SUMMER FUN sticker has dissolved into white pulp on the side of the pistol.

Then I walk back. Not to class. To the toilets by the maths corridor. I lock myself in the middle cubicle and sit on the lid with the pistol in my lap. I look at it. I look at my hands. I look at the graffiti on the door. *Felix is a melt.* *Agreed.* Someone else, in biro: *Nobody cares.*

I sit there until the bell goes again. I don’t cry. I don’t know how to cry about this. It’s too small. It’s just water. It’s just a folder. It’s just a night bus I took because I thought someone was bleeding, and they weren’t, and they never were, and the only person who got hurt was me, standing in the rain with a toy in my hand, waiting for someone to tell me I did the right thing.
step_outputs.12:
The fire alarm goes during English. We’re doing King Lear, which feels appropriate but also too on the nose, like the universe is mocking me with tragedy. The bell is shrill and doesn’t stop. Everyone stands up too fast, chairs scraping. Miss Banks sighs and says single file to the assembly point. Nobody does single file. We pour out like water.

Outside it’s raining properly now. Not mist. Rain. The kind that gets in your eyes and makes everything the same grey. The assembly point is the astroturf but the astroturf is a lake, so we cluster on the concrete by the drama block. I don’t have a coat. My blazer is still damp from the bike sheds, and now the rain is hitting my scalp and running down my collar in cold lines. I’m shivering before we’ve even stopped moving.

Then someone laughs. A sharp, stupid sound. And then I see them—water pistols coming out of bags. Not everyone. Maybe six people. But it’s enough. The ban made it better. A Year 12 I don’t recognise pulls out a massive neon gun and shoots someone in the neck from three feet away. A girl near me gets hit in the ear and shrieks, but she’s laughing too. It’s not a battle. It’s not cinematic. It’s just damp chaos. Nobody knows who to shoot. People are just getting each other wet because they’re outside and already ruined, so why not.

I see Mr. Vance. He’s standing under the big oak tree trying to light a cigarette, which he’s not supposed to do on school grounds. He looks up at the alarm, then at the kids with their neon plastic, then back at his lighter. A Year 12—not even in the game, just some random kid—pulls out a water bottle and sprays it at his mate. The mate ducks. The water hits Mr. Vance square in the back.

Mr. Vance doesn’t move. He just stands there with his cigarette finally lit, water dripping down his tweed jacket, and he looks at the kid. The kid freezes. Mr. Vance takes a drag, wincing slightly as he bends his bad knee. “Right,” he says. But nobody hears him because the alarm is still going, and anyway, nobody cares what Mr. Vance thinks right now.

I back away. I’m near the drama block bins. They smell of black bags and old emulsion paint and the sweet rot of whatever the canteen threw out on Thursday. I want to go inside but the doors are locked because it’s a fire alarm. I lean against the wall. My shoes are full of water already. I can feel it squelching between my toes, cold and intimate.

Then Felix is there.

He’s got the Super Soaker. It’s the massive one, military-grade plastic, with a pump handle and a tank strapped to his back like a jetpack. He’s wearing his Head Boy badge over his blazer lapel. He sees me and his face lights up—not with hatred, but with that specific, vacant glee of someone who thinks they’re winning a game that nobody else cares about anymore.

“Robin,” he says. “You’re dead.”

I look at him. I think about the Nando’s receipt in my camera roll. I think about saying something cutting. You stole the money. You spent it on chicken. You’re a pathetic little thief and everyone knows.

But he’s already pumping the handle. The sound is mechanical and stupid. Chunk-chunk. Like a toy trying to sound serious.

“I wrote the rules,” Felix says. “Exempt till the semis. But you’re already dead in the game anyway. Astra got you. So this is just…”

He doesn’t finish the sentence. He pulls the trigger.

The water hits me in the neck. It’s cold and forceful and it goes straight down my front. He keeps going. He empties the tank into my chest, my face, my hair. I put my hands up but it doesn’t help. It goes up my nose. It goes in my ears. I can’t see. I’m choking on water in a schoolyard, leaning against bins, and nobody is looking because they’re all too busy being wet themselves.

He stops. The tank makes a gurgling sound and dies. He lets out that honking laugh of his. “Rekt,” he says. Actually says it out loud, like a noun.

I wipe my face. My eyes are stinging. My hair is plastered to my forehead in clumps. I open my mouth to say something—about the money, about the receipt, about anything at all—but what comes out is a cough. I cough water onto the pavement. It’s clear and it spatters on the concrete. Felix looks at it with mild disgust.

“Bit dramatic,” he says.

Then the alarm stops. The sudden quiet is worse than the noise. My ears ring.

I look up. Mr. Vance is standing there. His cigarette is gone—extinguished or pocketed, I don’t know. His jacket is wet at the back in a dark patch. Behind him, other teachers are emerging from doorways and tree cover. Miss Banks. Mr. Dhingra. They’re looking at the water pistols littering the ground like dropped toys. They’re looking at us.

Felix sees them too. He drops the Super Soaker. It lands on the concrete with a cheap plastic clatter and the tank splits slightly at the seam.

“Sir,” Felix says, loud, rolling his shoulders back. “Sir, it’s just banter. Just a bit of banter. Water fight tradition. Character building, sir. Builds character.”

Mr. Vance looks at him. Then at me. I’m dripping. There’s a puddle forming around my shoes, my own personal flood. My blazer is dark and heavy, pulling on my shoulders like someone’s hands. Water is running out of my hair and down my neck. I must look like I fell in a pond. I probably smell like bins.

Mr. Vance touches his bad knee with one hand. He does that when he’s stressed; I’ve noticed. He looks at Felix. He looks at the Year 12 who sprayed him. He looks at the six or seven other kids holding neon plastic, their grins fading in the grey light.

“Detention,” he says. “All of you.”

“But sir,” Felix says. “I didn’t even—”

“Life’s not fair,” Mr. Vance says. “Et cetera. Monday. After school. Main hall.”

He turns and walks away, limping slightly, water still dripping from his jacket hem in a slow, rhythmic patter. The other teachers follow. Miss Banks gives me a look as she passes—not anger, not pity, just the pure, blank exhaustion of someone who has seen too many damp children do too many stupid things. I look away.

Felix picks up his Super Soaker. The tank is definitely cracked now; it leaks as he lifts it. He looks at me with something that might be apology but is probably just inconvenience. “Your fault,” he says. “You got us caught.”

He walks off, slinging the broken gun over his shoulder like a trophy, his white trainers somehow still clean. I watch him go. My teeth are chattering.

I stand by the bins for another minute. The rain is easing off into that fine, hopeless drizzle again. People drift away toward the gates, pulling up hoods, lighting fags, their blazers steaming slightly in the damp air. I can’t go home like this. Mum will think I fell in a canal. She’ll ask questions and I don’t have answers that make sense.

I go to lost property. It’s a cupboard by reception that smells of forgotten things and damp wool. Mrs. Patel isn’t there—she’s probably dealing with the fire alarm paperwork, or sitting in her car, or crying in the staff toilet. The door’s unlocked. I go in.

There are blazers on hooks, some with names sewn into collars in shaky handwriting. Shoes in a milk crate. A lunchbox with something green and fuzzy inside. I find a blazer that looks roughly my size. It’s navy, wrong shade, with a crest from a different school—a bird holding a branch, or maybe a worm, I can’t tell. I put it on. It smells of Lynx Africa and mould. The lining is cold and slightly slimy against my wet shirt. But it’s dry. Or dryer than mine.

I walk out. The corridor is empty except for a cleaner mopping up the trail of water I’ve left from the door. I don’t apologise. My wet blazer is under my arm, dripping on the lino, leaving a dotted line behind me like a trail of evidence. I pass the trophy cabinet. Felix’s face is in a photo there from Year 10, holding a certificate for something—public speaking, probably, or saying “gents” with conviction. He’s smiling the same smile. The glass is smudged with someone’s fingerprints.

I walk to the bus stop. I don’t see Astra. I don’t see Cam. I just stand there in the wrong blazer, smelling someone else’s deodorant and rot, and wait for the 47. My hair is still dripping. I lean against the shelter and the metal is cold through the stolen blazer. I check my phone. The Bleedout group chat is quiet. Felix hasn’t posted the winner. Maybe there isn’t one. Maybe there never was.

The bus comes. I get on. I tap my card and it works first time, which feels like a small miracle. I sit at the back, dripping onto the seat, and I pull the wet blazer out from under my arm. It’s ruined. The biro stain, the lapel, the new dark patch from Felix’s Super Soaker. It’s heavy. I hold it in my lap like a dead thing and watch the town go past through the rain-streaked glass. The Spar. The shut kebab shop. The fox, or maybe a different fox, trotting across the empty car park like it owns the place.

I get off at my stop and walk home. The stolen blazer doesn’t fit right; the sleeves are too short and the shoulders pinch. I let myself in. The house is empty. Mum’s note is still on the counter, the fiver gone. I stand in the hallway and drip on the carpet. I don’t move for a long time. I just stand there, cold and stupid and alive, wearing another person’s clothes, smelling of mould and Africa.
step_outputs.13:
The Co-op on a Sunday evening is its own special hell. The lights are too bright and too yellow and they make everyone look like they’ve got jaundice. I’m restocking the sanitary aisle because Moira called in sick and I’m the only one who doesn’t argue when Derek asks. I stack the pads in their neat pink and green boxes, different absorbencies, different wings. I don’t read the labels. I just match the pictures. Blood on the packaging. Blood in the emoji. It’s all just red on white.

I do the reduced run at eight. The yellow stickers come out for the sandwiches that expire at midnight. I pick up a chicken and bacon one that’s gone from three pounds to ninety pence. The bread feels damp through the packaging. I buy it anyway, and a Coke from the fridge, and I eat them both in the stockroom on a stack of toilet-roll pallets. The Coke is too warm. The sandwich tastes of fridge.

My phone is on the pallet next to me. I pick it up and scroll to WhatsApp. The group is still there. Felix renamed it last night: “Legends Only.” There’s a new profile picture of him doing a thumbs-up in the mirror, his Head Boy badge visible, the Super Soaker cracked but still strapped to his back like a jetpack. There are messages I haven’t read. Someone posted a poll about whether the detention counts as a win. I don’t open them. I press and hold the chat, hit the mute button, and switch my phone to silent. The little crossed-out bell appears. Legends Only, silenced.

I’m licking mayonnaise off my thumb when the screen lights up.

Not the group chat. A text. Her name.

Astra.

Not emojis. Just words, black on green, sitting there.

*Sorry about your folder.*

I read it three times. The stockroom hums. The strip light above me flickers every forty seconds. I’ve timed it before. I stare at the text until the screen goes dark, then I press the home button and it lights up again.

*Sorry about your folder.*

I type.

*It’s fine.*

I stare at it. It’s not fine. It’s a lie. I delete it.

I type.

*Don’t care.*

Also a lie. The folder mattered. Not the folder. The water. The bike sheds. Her face. Delete.

I type.

*I thought you were dying.*

True. Too true. It sits there on the screen like an open wound, like something ugly I’ve dragged out into the light. I can see her reading it. I can see her face doing that thing, that tired thing. I delete it. The cursor blinks.

I type again.

*It’s fine.*

I press send. It ticks. Delivered. No reply.

I finish the sandwich. I throw the wrapper in the cardboard baler. The sound is loud and final, a mechanical crunch.

At half eight Derek lets me go. He doesn’t say anything about my hair, which is still weird from Friday, or the blazer I’m wearing, which is the wrong colour and smells of someone else’s life. He just nods. I nod back. The till beeps as he logs off.

Outside it’s raining again. Not hard. Just enough to make the pavement shine and the streetlights bleed. I walk to the bus stop because I can’t be bothered to walk the whole way home and I’ve still got the fiver Mum left, minus the ninety pence, minus the bus fare yesterday. I count my change as I walk. Two pound twenty. Enough for the bus. Enough for nothing else.

She’s there.

Astra. Under the shelter, hood up, looking at her phone. She doesn’t see me at first. I think about crossing the road. I think about walking past. I think about pretending I haven’t seen her. But my feet keep going and then I’m under the shelter too and the rain is drumming on the plastic roof and she looks up.

We stand there.

Four minutes. I count them. The digital display behind her says the 47 is due in six. She puts her phone in her pocket. I put my hands in my pockets. The wrong blazer is too tight across the shoulders. I hunch. She doesn’t hunch. She just stands there, looking out at the road, or the rain, or nothing.

I could say something. I could say, “The folder was shit anyway.” I could say, “It’s fine.” I could say, “Why did you really send it?” I don’t. The words are in my throat but they taste like that sandwich, like damp bread and old mayo, and I swallow them back down.

A car goes past too fast and sprays the curb. We both step back without meaning to, synchronized, two people who used to know each other’s rhythms. She doesn’t look at me. I don’t look at her. But I can see her in the glass of the shelter, reflected, faint, a ghost of a girl with eyeliner smudged at the corner. She looks tired. She looks like she’s been somewhere else before this, arguing about a prescription or staring at a wet wall.

The bus comes. Not ours. The 23. It stops and a woman gets off with a trolley and the bus pulls away, leaving exhaust and a puddle that spreads toward my shoe.

Astra’s bus arrives. The 47. It squeals to a stop in front of us, blocking the rain with its bulk. The doors open with a hiss of hydraulics. She steps forward. She doesn’t say goodbye. She doesn’t say see you. She doesn’t look at me. She just gets on, tapping her card, and walks down the aisle past the empty seats, and sits on the left side, three rows back. I can see her through the window. She puts her bag on her lap. She looks at her phone.

The doors close. The bus pulls away. She doesn’t wave. I don’t wave. I just stand there.

My phone buzzes.

I take it out. A notification. A text. No name, or maybe a name, or maybe a number I don’t have saved. It doesn’t matter who it’s from. The content is the same. Three red drops in a row.

🩸🩸🩸

I look at them. They’re bright against the dark mode of my screen. They could mean anything. They could mean nothing. They could be a game, or a cry for help, or a wrong number, or a final joke, or just the automatic reflex of someone who doesn’t know how to say what they mean. They could be from Astra, looking back at me from the bus window. They could be from Felix, blasting the same message to everyone in his broken group. They could be from no one. They could be for someone else.

I hold the phone in my hand. The rain is getting in around my collar. My thumb hovers over the keyboard. I could type back. I could send three of my own. I could call. I could get on the next bus. I could keep running toward the blood, every time, forever, spending my last pounds on night fares for people who don’t need saving.

I don’t.

I press the power button. The screen goes black. The emojis disappear. I put the phone in my pocket, deep in the lining where I can’t feel it buzz, and I start walking.

I walk past the closed Nando’s. The lights are off but the logo still glows, red and yellow, a bright bird in the dark window. I think about Felix in there, maybe, with his rugby lot, with his twenty-three pounds and forty pence. I think about the receipt in my camera roll, my thumb in the corner, the blurred evidence of nothing.

I keep walking. The rain gets heavier. The wrong blazer sticks to my back. I pass the Spar, the shut kebab shop, the car park where the fox was. I don’t see it tonight. Maybe it’s somewhere dry. Maybe it’s dead. Maybe it was never there.

I walk home. The house is dark. Mum’s note is still on the counter, the fiver gone. I take off the blazer and hang it on the back of the chair. It drips slightly on the lino. I leave it there. I go to my room. I lie on my bed. I don’t turn on the light.

My phone stays in my pocket. It doesn’t buzz again. Outside, the rain keeps coming down, washing the streets clean, or not clean, just wet. I close my eyes. I don’t sleep. I just lie there, breathing, alive, stupid, fine. The emojis are in my pocket, three drops of blood in the dark, waiting. I don’t answer them. I don’t delete them. I just let them sit there, unread, until the battery dies.

[Analysis]

This is a remarkably accomplished piece of darkly comic British YA fiction. The author has constructed a coherent, emotionally resonant narrative across eight chapters that maintains consistent voice, character, and thematic concerns throughout. Let me examine it critically.

STRENGTHS:

The voice is the piece's greatest achievement. Robin's first-person narration is pitch-perfect for the genre: self-deprecating, observant, economically precise. Lines like "I am never careful" and "I've got the patience of someone who can't afford alternatives" feel genuinely earned rather than performed. The class consciousness is woven throughout without being didactic — the £1.80 bus fare, the two pound thirty-four in the bank, the fiver Mum leaves on the counter, the meal deal receipt — these accumulate into a portrait of material precarity that grounds the emotional stakes.

The central conceit is clever and well-executed: the blood emoji that triggers a genuine crisis of care, only to be revealed as a game, which then becomes a vehicle for exploring why Robin cares so much and whether caring is itself a kind of pathology. The story never resolves this cleanly, which is its greatest strength. The ending — Robin choosing not to respond to the second set of blood emojis — is genuinely earned and emotionally complex.

CHARACTER:

Robin is nuanced and consistent. His self-awareness about his own caring ("like I'm the only person who shows up") is painful and real. He knows he's being an idiot but can't stop. Astra is more difficult to assess — she's deliberately opaque, and the story commits to keeping her that way. Her line "I didn't think anyone would come. And then you did, and you were standing in the garden, and you looked at me like — like I owed you something" is the emotional core of the piece and it lands. She's not a villain, not a victim, just someone who sends distress signals and then resents the response. This is psychologically true and uncomfortable.

Cam is a minor character but well-drawn — the silent, competent foil who offers companionship without sentimentality. Felix is the weakest character, functioning more as a comic device than a person, though his Nando's receipt revelation is genuinely funny and the detail of him spending the money before the game even starts is sharp.

PACING:

The pacing is generally strong. The first chapter is the best — the night bus sequence is tightly controlled and the reveal lands well. Chapters 2-5 maintain momentum through the school setting. Chapter 6 (the bike shed confrontation) is the emotional climax and is well-placed. Chapters 7 and 8 feel slightly elongated — the fire alarm sequence in Chapter 7 is entertaining but somewhat diffuse, and the Co-op scene in Chapter 8, while atmospherically strong, slows the resolution. The ending is quiet and appropriate but the journey to it in the final two chapters loses some of the earlier precision.

DIALOGUE:

The dialogue is largely excellent — sparse, naturalistic, loaded with subtext. "You're the only one who came" lands differently each time it appears. The exchange in the disabled toilet is the piece's best scene. Felix's dialogue is slightly too on-the-nose ("Builds character" repeated, "Rekt" said aloud) but this is intentional comic characterization and mostly works.

WEAKNESSES:

The piece occasionally reaches for metaphor when the plain prose is doing better work. "The words are in my throat but they taste like that sandwich, like damp bread and old mayo" is a slightly strained comparison. "Like a dead thing" for the blazer is a bit much. The fox appearing and reappearing as a motif is handled with appropriate lightness but the final "Maybe it was never there" is the closest the piece comes to purple prose — a slightly too-neat symbolic gesture.

The Bleedout game as a plot mechanism is clever but the resolution (or non-resolution) of the Felix subplot feels abandoned rather than concluded. The receipt photo going viral-but-not is realistic but the narrative thread simply drops. This is arguably intentional — the story is about Robin's emotional life, not about justice — but it leaves a slight structural looseness.

Some of the metaphors are genuinely excellent ("the specific, shrinking feeling of being the only person in the room who thought this was important") while others are slightly forced ("the words never do. They sit in my throat like stones" — this is a cliché). The piece is not consistently at the same level throughout, with the later chapters showing slightly more strain.

The "darkly comic" element is present but the comedy is mostly situational (the leaking water pistol, the Nando's receipt, Mr. Vance getting soaked) rather than deeply integrated into the prose voice. This is fine but the piece leans more toward dark than comic as it progresses.

OVERALL:

This is a genuinely impressive piece of YA fiction — coherent, emotionally intelligent, with a distinctive voice and real psychological insight. It's not a masterpiece (some structural looseness, occasional metaphor strain, Felix underdeveloped) but it's well above average and demonstrates real craft.

DIALOGUE: This is where the chapter genuinely excels. The exchange in the disabled toilet is the best writing in the piece. "Because I'm always fine. That's the point." is devastating in its simplicity. "You're not my mate anymore" said to the wall rather than to Robin is exactly the kind of oblique, inarticulate grief the plan promised. The dialogue doesn't over-explain; it circles the wound without naming it. Astra's "You could've known I was fine" / "How?" / "Because I'm always fine" is a genuinely good three-line exchange that earns its emotional weight.

CHARACTER CONSISTENCY: Both Robin and Astra are consistent with their profiles. Astra's inability to apologise, her testing-by-pushing-away, her re-applied eyeliner as armour—all present and correct. Robin's fixation on the £1.80, the cheese roll in the pocket, the inability to say what they mean—all consistent. The detail about Astra's scab on her index finger, the bitten thumbnail, mirrors Robin's own cuticle-picking from the profile. This is a nice touch that suggests shared self-destructive habits without stating it.

CHAPTER PLAN ADHERENCE: The plan called for: ketchup incident, Mr. Vance slipping, assembly banning the game, Robin finding Astra in the disabled toilet dabbing at ketchup, Robin offering a wet wipe, argument about the night bus, nothing resolved, Robin washing hands for a long time. All of this is present. The chapter follows its plan faithfully without feeling mechanical.

WEAKNESSES: The hand-washing ending is the chapter's most obvious risk. "I wash them until they're raw and the water running off them is clean and I can't feel my fingertips anymore" is the closest the chapter comes to purple prose—it's reaching for symbolic resonance (cleansing, numbness, the futility of washing away the encounter) in a way that slightly violates the plan's anti-LLM principle of avoiding over-articulated interiority. It's not egregious, but it's the moment where the prose becomes most self-conscious. The plan said Robin "washes their hands for a very long time"—the execution extends this into something slightly more portentous than the plan intended.

The Vance scene is well-executed but the assembly scene is slightly perfunctory—the Head's speech about "mayonnaise" is a good joke, but the scene moves quickly and doesn't quite have the texture of the rest of the chapter.

EMOTIONAL ENGAGEMENT: The toilet scene is genuinely moving without being sentimental. "You're not my mate anymore" landing as a statement of fact rather than an accusation is exactly right. The chapter earns its darkness through restraint.

FORCED POETRY: Mostly avoided. "A damaged rocking horse" for Vance's gait is slightly strained but not offensive. The hand-washing ending is the main offender.

UNSURPRISING/UNCREATIVE: The disabled toilet as the location for the confrontation is a slightly predictable choice for this genre, but the execution is fresh enough to overcome it. The ketchup-as-blood visual echo (ketchup stain on white shirt, blood on Astra's thumb) is a nice unforced parallel.

OVERALL: This is a confident, well-executed chapter that delivers on its plan and maintains a distinctive, consistent voice. Its weaknesses are minor—a slightly overwrought ending, a perfunctory assembly scene—but its strengths are considerable: sharp dialogue, consistent characterisation, and a tonal control that keeps the comedy and the sadness in productive tension.

[Analysis]

This chapter is a strong piece of work that largely delivers on the plan's promise of anti-climax as emotional truth. Let me examine it carefully across the relevant dimensions.

**Voice and Characterisation**

Robin's voice is consistent and well-maintained throughout. The detail of the SUMMER FUN sticker not being removed because Robin "didn't look at it properly until I was outside, and then I couldn't be bothered to go back" is exactly the kind of petty, self-defeating logic the character profile demands. The physical specificity is excellent: the hole in the trainer, the water soaking through, the pistol clicking empty. These are not decorative details but load-bearing ones that communicate Robin's state without announcing it.

Astra is handled with real skill. Her phone call about the prescription is a masterstroke of contextualisation — she arrives in the scene already depleted, already in a different argument, and Robin's "assassination" lands in the middle of someone else's exhaustion. Her line "I didn't think anyone would come. And then you did" is the emotional core of the chapter and it lands because it's been earned by the preceding action. She is not villainous, not sympathetic in a clean way — she is genuinely complicated, which matches her profile precisely.

**Dialogue**

The dialogue is the chapter's strongest element. "You don't know me anymore, Rob. You don't get to show up at midnight because you think I'm dying. I'm not your thing to save" — this is sharp, character-specific, and does not over-explain. It reveals Astra's psychology (the testing, the pushing away, the resentment of being cared for) without narrating it. Robin's responses are appropriately inadequate: "You sent blood. Three times. What was I meant to think?" The flatness of this exchange, the way neither character says what they actually mean, is exactly what the plan called for.

The one slight weakness is that Astra's speech about "I don't know — that I'm a drama queen? That I'm a mess? That I was pissed and it seemed funny?" is perhaps slightly more self-aware and articulate than her profile strictly allows. She is described as someone who cannot apologise, who cannot ask for help directly — and here she is doing a fairly lucid post-mortem on her own behaviour. It's not a serious failure, but it edges toward the over-articulated interiority the plan explicitly wanted to avoid.

**The Central Scene**

The moment of the "kill" is handled with genuine craft. The water hitting the folder rather than Astra is a perfect physical metaphor that doesn't announce itself as a metaphor — it simply happens, and the consequences (the blooming ink, the ruined essay, the extension she'll have to ask for) are concrete and real. The gap between Robin's imagined cinematic scene and the actual muddy reality is exactly the comedy-darkness blend the plan promised.

The aftermath — Robin in the cubicle, the graffiti, the empty pistol clicking — is well-executed. "Felix is a melt. Agreed. Nobody cares." is a nice touch. The final paragraph is the chapter's most ambitious moment and mostly succeeds: "It's too small. It's just water. It's just a folder. It's just a night bus I took because I thought someone was bleeding, and they weren't, and they never were, and the only person who got hurt was me, standing in the rain with a toy in my hand, waiting for someone to tell me I did the right thing." This is good. The repetition of "just" is controlled, the self-pity is acknowledged without being indulged, and the final image is earned.

**Potential Weaknesses**

There are moments where the prose reaches slightly too hard. "She walks out from under the bike shed, into the grey, and her hood slips further down, and she doesn't fix it" — the hood detail is fine, but the accumulation of small symbolic gestures (the hood, the vanilla smell, the rhythmless footsteps) starts to feel slightly curated, as if the author is arranging a shot rather than recording an observation. It doesn't tip into purple prose, but it's close.

The description of the bike sheds — "the sweet, rotten smell of mud that's been rained on too many times" — is slightly overwrought. Mud doesn't smell sweet and rotten in quite this way; it's reaching for atmosphere in a way that the rest of the prose, which is more grounded, doesn't need.

The chapter follows its plan faithfully: Astra on the phone about a prescription, Robin waiting, the shot hitting the folder, the ruined coursework, Astra's "you proper ruined my night" line, the hollow kill. All present and correctly weighted.

**Overall Assessment**

This is accomplished, controlled writing that understands its own project. The comedy and darkness are genuinely integrated rather than alternating. The characters behave consistently with their profiles. The dialogue is the best element. The prose occasionally over-reaches but rarely badly. The emotional register — hollow rather than cathartic — is maintained throughout and feels genuinely earned rather than performed.
